speechtext:

Whereas the Government of Canada has a well-known policy of accepting refugees; whereas Tibetans, having been forced out of their own country, are now under tremendous pressure and harassment to leave Bhut-tan; whereas Tibetans have proven themselves to be fine, industrious citizens of Canada, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn):

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Yesterday's Toronto Star carried a very disturbing story about a speech given by the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. Gilchrist) to the Alliance for the Preservation of English in Canada, in which he went on record as supporting separatism in Quebec and in which he appeared to condone a threat against the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). I believe all hon. members will agree that such inflammatory statements should be abhorred. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Willowdale (Mr. Peterson):
That the hon. member for Scarborough East should apologize to all the members of this House and to the Prime Minister.

That this House direct the Leader of the Opposition to follow the lead of his predecessor, the Hon. subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CONVENING OF FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE
speechtext:
My
question is directed to the Prime Minister, whom I first want to congratulate on receiving what he would regard as good news from the superior court of Quebec-

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CONVENING OF FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE
speechtext: Court of appeal.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CONVENING OF FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE
speechtext: -court of appeal? Court of appeal. I feel that the legal questions should be decided by the courts, and I am pleased that Parliament is agreeing to let that happen.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CONVENING OF FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CONVENING OF FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE
speechtext: My question concerns the other part of the process. It concerns the meeting here tomorrow of premiers of eight provinces to conclude their proposal for patriation of our Constitution, with an amending formula. The Prime Minister knows that in the telex to him from Premier Lyon there was a request for a meeting with the Prime Minister after the premiers had met for joint consideration of the new plan. If the Prime Minister receives such a proposal from those eight provinces, will he arrange to convene a first ministers' conference to consider that proposal?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CONVENING OF FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would have thought that the Leader of the Opposition would be somewhat hesitant to speak on behalf of the provinces in this matter. The last time he raised it in the House, it was to enjoin me to meet with the eight premiers meeting here in Ottawa. When, after some hesitation-considerable hesitation, I would say-I accepted to meet with them, then it appeared that they did not want to meet me. So I think
the Leader of the Opposition had better let the premiers handle this, and stay out of this business, himself.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CONVENING OF FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CONVENING OF FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE
speechtext:
The Prime Minister will want to consult the record to know just how wrong his rendition of history is, although he does confirm that he would prefer to have Parliament stay out of questions which are Parliament's business. My question to him stands. There is to be a meeting here tomorrow which the eight premiers involved believe will yield a new plan for bringing our Constitution home with an amending formula. They have formally requested the Prime Minister of Canada for an opportunity to discuss that plan with him. They have requested that in the telex in which they said:
Subsequently we hope to meet you-
That means the Prime Minister.
-for joint consideration of the new plan.
That is in the telex from Premier Lyon.
If there is a new plan brought forward, as the premiers expect there will be, will the Prime Minister of Canada agree to meet with them to discuss that plan, and will the Prime Minister consider convening a first ministers' conference to discuss that plan by which Canadians could patriate our Constitution and amend it here in an agreed way, and any other questions which he might want to put on the agenda? Will he convene a first ministers' conference if there is a proposal from those eight premiers tomorrow?

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CONVENING OF FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition is making the same mistake which he made two weeks ago when he enjoined me to meet with the premiers to discuss something with them, to hear them out and to have a federal-provincial meeting of some sort. I repeat, it was after he had said that and pressed me-presumably, on behalf of the premiers-to meet and to discuss with them, it appeared that they did not want to meet and discuss with me. That is still the situation now.
The Leader of the Opposition says that Premier Lyon has sent me a telegram wherein he says he wants to discuss their plan with me. I have the telegram here, and the only part of it which refers to myself is in the final words. I read them:
It is our intention to communicate the conclusions of the meeting to you on the afternoon of the same day.
That does not sound as though they want to have a discussion with me.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CONVENING OF FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE
speechtext: Read it all.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CONVENING OF FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE
speechtext:
It sounds to me as though they are having a meeting in Ottawa, that they will try to discuss and hopefully agree amongst themselves, presumably to put the final touches on something which has not yet been quite agreed to. That is why I repeat, what I said last week in this House, that the veracity of the statement to the effect that they had reached an agreement was somewhat in doubt. It has been put in doubt since then by several of the participants who have said that
April 15, 1981

they still have some decisions to make. Premier Levesque said that, and Premier Blakeney said that, so the Leader of the Opposition in this House really is carrying a brief for some who have not asked him to carry it for them.
I will be in Ottawa tomorrow. I am not sure how the intention of communicating the conclusions of the meeting to me will be fulfilled. I do not know if Premier Lyon wants to see me. I do not know if he will send me a letter-

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CONVENING OF FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CONVENING OF FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE
speechtext: What is beefing you, my friend?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CONVENING OF FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member does not have the floor.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CONVENING OF FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE
speechtext: Who the hell cares?

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CONVENING OF FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CONVENING OF FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE
speechtext: I can understand the frustration of members of the House when the Prime Minister twice refuses to answer a very simple question having to do with his duty to the people of this country, as the first minister of Canada.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CONVENING OF FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CONVENING OF FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE
speechtext:
On April 3 Premier Lyon, the chairman of the provincial premiers' conference, sent a telex from which I have already quoted in the House, to the Prime Minister, in which he outlined the plan of the premiers to meet first and then, and again I quote, "Subsequently we hope to meet you for joint consideration of the new plan".
I am not particularly interested in debating with the Prime Minister what happened last week. What I am interested in knowing is whether the Prime Minister will accept his responsibilities as Prime Minister of this country, to resolve in a Canadian way, and in co-operation with the Canadian partners, the provinces, a question of important constitutional significance.
If there is the agreement the premiers expect tomorrow, will the Prime Minister use that agreement as the basis for exercising his duty and convening a first ministers' conference that will allow him and the ten first ministers of the country-the ten provincial premiers-allow the 11 first ministers to sit down and discuss a Canadian patriation package, with a Canadian amending formula? Will he do his duty in that way if he receives that kind of plan?

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CONVENING OF FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, could I ask the indulgence of the House to recall the events which led up to this question.
I was enjoined by the Leader of the Opposition to meet with the premiers. I said I would do it. Then a few of them, several I believe, said that they did not want to meet me. They said this publicly. This is not a figment of my imagination. They said they were not sure that I was invited. Some said that I could bang at the door but they would not let me in.
Oral Questions
Since then I have received a telegram-that is not referring to the April 3 one because it was after the April 3 one that I said that I would meet with them. Then it appeared that they did not all want to meet with me. They had not made up their minds yet about what they would do.
Ad hon. Member: No wonder.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CONVENING OF FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Well, no wonder, all right. But they had not made up their minds.
Since then I have received a telegram telling me that it is their intention to communicate the conclusions of their meeting to me. I repeat, I had been prepared to meet with them. Now I am prepared to receive their communication in whatever way it comes. I will be here in Ottawa; I will be available, if one or several want to meet with me to communicate the conclusions. That was made clear ten days ago, that I was prepared to meet with them. I will see what they have agreed to do among themselves. Once again whether they will meet-

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CONVENING OF FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE
speechtext: If they agree.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CONVENING OF FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE
speechtext:
If they agree-whether they will want to meet or to send me a letter or what, but I am quite sure that the Leader of the Opposition will also be informed of the position that they take, if any.
The Leader of the Opposition knows the rules to which this House has agreed, that after today we will have Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday, and Monday to consider what we want to do with this proposal presumably of eight premiers.
I do not think that the Leader of the Opposition is suggesting that in these five days we convene a federal-provincial conference. If the premiers indicate their desire to do so, and if a quick canvassing of my colleagues from the other two provinces indicate that they want to do so, certainly I will convene a conference in these five days if there is some measure of agreement. But the way we have written the House order is that on Tuesday evening we must make any final change we want to make to this resolution that is before the House.
The deadline is on the premiers, it is on myself, and it is also on the Leader of the Opposition. I take it that his party will see it as its duty to reflect on the meeting of the premiers. Hopefully the Leader of the Opposition will be communicated with also by the premiers in some way or other. Then his party, my party, and the New Democratic Party will make up their minds as to whether we can include something in the resolution by way of amendment on Tuesday. That is the way the House has accepted to play the rules.
I do not want to encourage the Leader of the Opposition to believe that in these five days we could easily have a conference of 11 first ministers. Two of them have already stated quite clearly that they did not want to meet if it was a matter of just looking at an amending formula without a charter. I must say that is the position of our party too. But still we will

April 15, 1981
Oral Questions
meet with them. Hopefully they will have made some progress. We will see what they say, even on the charter. Then the Leader of the Opposition and the other parties in this House will take their responsibilities for Tuesday night.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we have made some progress. The Prime Minister is now agreeing to a first ministers' conference if that is requested by the eight premiers and if they bring forward a plan. But he has placed a limitation on it. The Prime Minister has agreed to a first ministers' conference within the next five days. I think most of us recognize that that is probably going to be impractical-desirable if possible, but probably impractical.
Is the Prime Minister limiting his suggestion, his willingness to convene a first ministers' conference, to the next five days or the next week? Or is he prepared to tell this House of Commons that whatever happens in the parliamentary agenda, whatever happens with the Supreme Court agenda, he will do his duty as the Prime Minister of the whole country and convene a first ministers' conference to discuss a patriation package agreed to by eight provinces if those eight provinces request such a meeting? Will he do that without time limitations?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Of course I will, Madam Speaker. The resolution before the House specifies an obligation on us to do that. It is specified that over the next two years we must have first ministers' conferences to try to get agreement on an amending formula. The Leader of the Opposition says no.
No. I am shaking my head at your behaviour.

It does, Madam Speaker. The Leader of the Opposition wants to have an undertaking from me that I will have a federal provincial conference. I am answering that I will be obliged to do so once we adopt this resolution.
If we do.

I guess the Leader of the Opposition wants to know when it will be held. It will be held in the next five days if we all agree it is useful. If it is not, the Leader of the Opposition accepted the proposition before the House that we want the Supreme Court to see the resolution in its final form. That is the essence of the bargain we made here, that there would be no further amendments after Thursday night, that the Supreme Court would be rendering its decision on the basis of the resolution as it will have been amended next week.
If the Leader of the Opposition is asking me if I will meet the premiers, the answer is yes, Madam Speaker. But I think that the Leader of the Opposition and the premiers themselves should realize that such a meeting will not be able to affect the resolution before the House by the very nature of the bargain that the Leader of the Opposition wrung out of us. speechtext:

speechtext:
that Bill C-61, respecting young offenders and to repeal the Juvenile Delinquents Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Madam Speaker, this is the first bill I have had the opportunity to present as Solicitor General. Indeed I am very proud to be able to bring forward Bill C-61, respecting young offenders and to repeal the Juvenile Delinquents Act.
At the outset I must say that this bill did not originate with me. Indeed, the legislation it is replacing is 73 years old; it has been virtually unchanged over that period, but not unexamined. Within the last 14 years and, more intensively, within the last nine years, there have been steady examinations of it and consultations about it between the levels of government. Because of the large number of solicitors general of Canada in the last five or six years, possibly none of them has been in a position to review the provisions and bring forward a bill which they would have been prepared to explain, defend and discuss with the provinces in the final sense.
Having now had the opportunity to be Solicitor General for a year and one month, I have been able to put myself in a position to bring this bill forward as my own recommendation to cabinet and to the House and I look forward to a full examination of it. I hope it may even be possible today to refer it to the justice committee so that it can be examined in depth and that the many experts across the country who are interested in this bill, and who have been consulted about it, will be able to come before the committee, make their views known and give their advice with respect to the bill. Although the bill merits considerable discussion, and I know it is of considerable interest to many, I hope it may be possible to refer it to the justice committee today.
I expect the bill will enjoy substantial support. I think the views presented to the committee will greatly illuminate discussion by Members of Parliament. That is why I think a
Young Offenders Act
relatively short period of time should be devoted to second reading and then the bill could be referred to committee.
As I indicated, this new legislation will repeal the Juvenile Delinquents Act, which is now seriously out of date and out of time with contemporary practices and attitudes regarding juvenile justice. It is inadequate to meet the current problems of young persons in conflict with the law. The proposed legislation, which is aimed at providing an updated and comprehensive process to deal with juvenile crime which encourages both respect for the law and protects the well-being of both the young offender and society, is long overdue.
The new legislation, which is to be known as the Young Offenders Act, is the result of extensive study and consultation by the federal government with the provinces, academics, professionals and practitioners in the juvenile justice field, as well as major associations and groups, private agencies and the general public. I acknowledge that all of this consultation has had a major impact on formulating the underlying principles and the over-all substance of this legislation.
Despite the fact that this basic approach was developed out of a sense of benevolence and welfare, many are now of the opinion that treatment and rehabilitation can no longer stand on their own to serve or protect the better interests of children in a system which deals with offenders under the authority of the criminal law. It is further argued that, as society insists more and more on responsibility on the part of the young offender, his right to fair treatment in accordance with the principles of natural justice can no longer be left, as they have been under the present law, to the discretion of those persons in authority.
I believe that we should no longer condone by prolonging the existence of the Juvenile Delinquents Act injustices and shortcomings such as the following: discrimination against young persons by unnecessarily criminalizing them for various acts and behaviour which are not illegal for adults and which in most instances more properly belong to the domain of child welfare and youth protection legislation. I refer, for example, to the offence of being a juvenile delinquent, which is an offence under the existing law. It is very vague in its nature and it is sometimes used in parts of our country to deal with, for example, a young person who will not tell his parents where he goes at night and why he has money in his pocket. It is the type of offence which is too vague and not in keeping with modern ideas of young people having equal rights as adults have.
The second difficulty is the subjection under the existing law to indeterminate court sentences which may not be related to the seriousness of the offence committed and which may be more severe than the sentence an adult would receive for committing the same offence.
Another shortcoming is the subjection of young persons to an arbitrary review process whereby they may be brought back before the court at any time until they reach the age of 21, when new sanctions can be applied against them without new offences having been committed, including a belated transfer

April 15, 1981
Young Offenders Act
to adult court. This, in effect, is double jeopardy which applies under the existing law.
The final point I want to refer to is the subjection of young persons to informal court procedures and decision-making which do not guarantee them the right to legal counsel or a full opportunity to challenge their accusers and participate in decisions which affect them.
While I could go on, I prefer to limit the listing to the most obvious inequities and deficiencies. In so doing I want to assure hon. members that it is not my intention to impart the impression that such represents a description of the daily practice of juvenile courts in the country, but rather I would point out that some of these inherent weaknesses in the existing law have a tremendous potential for abuse and arbitrary action. Credit should be paid to juvenile judges and provincial administrators who, in most instances, have extended to young persons rights which are well beyond those provided by the letter of the law and which will be taken account of on a fundamentally secure, judicial basis under the proposed legislation.
The proposed legislation blends three principles. The first is that young people should be held more responsible for their behaviour, but not wholly accountable since they are not yet fully mature and are dependent on others. The second point is that society has a right to protection from illegal behaviour, even though committed by a minor. The third point is that young persons have the same rights to due process of law, natural justice and fair and equal treatment as adults, and that these rights must be guaranteed by special safeguards. Thus, the bill is intended to strike a reasonable and acceptable balance between the needs of young offenders and the interests of society.
I would like to highlight some of the provisions contained in the proposed legislation which seek to implement these principles. A significant feature of the proposed young offenders legislation is the abolition of the omnibus offence of delinquency itself. Under the new legislation, a young person would only be charged with a specific offence against the Criminal Code of Canada or other federal statutes and regulations. Misbehaviour, which presently constitutes the so-called "status offences", would no longer be an offence under the act. This proposal more realistically reflects the jurisdictional responsibilities of the federal and provincial governments under the Constitution. As well, it reflects the practice developed in many jurisdictions of decriminalizing behaviour which is seen as not being sufficiently serious to rationalize its continued inclusion under criminal law.
The age of criminal responsibility would be raised from seven years of age to 12. I firmly believe that the age of seven is much too young an age at which to attribute criminal responsibility. Children so young should more realistically be the subject of non-criminal proceedings such as child neglect and protection proceedings. I think I ought to note that there is, I believe, unanimous agreement among provincial attorneys general about this particular provision.
Under the existing law the provinces enjoy the flexibility of having the maximum age of jurisdiction set at any level, varying from under 16 to 18 years of age. Accordingly, the maximum age now varies across Canada. While promoting a maximum age of under 18 years, the new legislation will continue to allow the federal government to vary the maximum age at under 16 or 17 years at the request of a province. The most common criticism levelled against the new legislation is the lack of a fixed, uniform age for the entire country. Although it is clearly the preferred position of the federal government that uniformity should prevail, and many provinces agree with this concept, it has become abundantly clear as a result of the consultation process that there is no agreement and that it is impossible to achieve agreement on a uniform maximum age to apply across the country.
Provinces cannot agree on what that maximum age should be for dealing with young persons in a specialized juvenile justice system, both for philosophical and practical reasons. Differences exist as to when an individual is or should be considered sufficiently mature to be held responsible and dealt with as an adult. Practically speaking, due to the specialized programs, resources and services which are in place to deal with young offenders, considerable program shifts and adjustments would be required if the maximum age, which is under 18, were to be made uniform. Accordingly, it is proposed that the flexible upper limit be retained. Nevertheless, as a standard I hope the provinces-those who do not presently do so- will consider moving toward the age of under 18, as has been suggested by the federal government.
One particular feature of the proposed legislation is the acknowledgement that alternative measures to the court process can be used at appropriate times and in appropriate cases. It has been recognized for some time that many persons are brought to court unnecessarily when other effective ways may exist to deal with them and their behaviour problems. Such alternatives which have become popularized in the form of screening and diversion are not intended as a substitute for the judicial process, but rather to provide additional options for dealing with young persons who commit offences.
Informal and discretionary pre-judicial processes have become part and parcel of juvenile justice policy and administration in Canada. Police discretion, for instance, has for years been a fundamental cornerstone in the administration of justice. Probation and social service personnel make and accept referrals and undertake to initiate alternative agreements and programs with offenders, all in the interest of settling disputes and avoiding the utilization of formal court proceedings. Such approaches not only avoid unnecessary referral to the courts, but can offer the young person the opportunity to accept responsibility for his behaviour and become voluntarily involved in the resolution of his wrongdoing, frequently with the victim being involved.
However, we have been equally conscious of the controversy which exists between individuals and groups who espouse the
April 15, 1981

informal versus the formal disposition of juvenile cases. There remain many concerns about the inherent dangers of exercising unfettered discretion in the application of diversion programs and to make sure that informality not trench upon the basic legal rights of young persons and their equitable treatment.
One of the criticisms of the new law has been to the effect that the federal government should have made diversion mandatory and more explicit. But the proponents of such arguments fail to recognize the importance to the young person of having the right to plead not guilty and the role of the provinces in the exercise of prosecutorial discretion. The use of alternative measures, in my opinion, is better left to the discretion of provinces which can develop programs to suit their particular circumstances.
For these and other reasons, including the belief that there is yet much to learn through experience about the diversion concept itself, new legislation does not prescribe any formal model or mechanism of diversion. While the legislation will sanction such practices in law, it will leave it to the provinces to decide what type of diversion programs will be implemented. Of particular importance, however, is the fact that the legislation does contain a number of conditions and safeguards which must be applied so as to protect young persons against potential abuses and arbitrary action. For example, that the young person must freely consent to participate and retains the option, at any time, of having the matter dealt with by a court; that the young person has the right to consult legal counsel before agreeing to any diversion program; and that alternative measures are not to be used in any case unless there exists sufficient evidence to proceed with the prosecution of an offence.
Another of the deficiencies of the existing law is in regard to its disposition or sentencing provisions. The proposed legislation will directly address the outdated and inadequate features of present sentencing policies by furnishing the youth court with a range of dispositions which delineate not only the over-all shift in the philosophy of the proposed act, but, more specifically, address currently accepted sentencing principles. Accordingly, the new legislation proposes a precisely defined range of sentencing options which will take into account the special circumstances and needs of young persons, while allowing sufficient scope and flexibility to provide for the rights and needs of victims of crime and address the need to protect society in appropriate cases.
Increased emphasis will be placed on formalizing in law community-based dispositions, such as community service, compensation and restitution orders, as methods of promoting, on the part of the offender, a greater sense of responsibility and understanding for his illegal behaviour, while at the same time attempting to promote reconciliation between offender and victim. These dispositions would be in addition to those of a supervisory nature, such as probation orders, where special conditions and requirements could be attached to meet the assessed needs and concerns both of the individual and also the community. Other dispositions would include an absolute dis-
Young Offenders Act
charge or the application of a fine which, under the proposed legislation, could reach a maximum limit of $1,000 as compared to the limit in the existing law of $25. In effect, the option of a fine, which is a very efficient form of punishment where appropriate, has really been unavailable because of the low ceiling imposed by the existing law which causes it to be a type of penalty that is not very meaningful.
Under the new legislation, the use of custody will be seen as a final resort which, when contemplated, is to be exercised with the utmost restraint. When it is being considered, it should reflect the seriousness of factors attendant to a specific offence or offences. Custodial dispositions will therefore only be given after very careful consideration, since they represent a radical restriction of a young person's freedom.
The youth court judge who is considering custody for an offender must request a predisposition report. Reasons must be given by the court for all dispositions. Custodial dispositions will be for definite periods of time but may not exceed two years in duration for a given offence, nor can they exceed the maximum period for which an adult could be sentenced for the same offence.
With regard to custody, it is important to note that the definition thereof is very broad, allowing a province to designate a variety of custodial facilities ranging from detention or containment centres to wilderness camps, community training residences or group homes. The essential feature in regard to all custodial facilities is that the young person's access to the community is restricted.
While the new legislation recognizes that the youth court is the authority which should decide whether young persons will be committed to custody, it also recognizes that there must be some built-in flexibility to allow the director of the provincial services plan to implement effective programs. Therefore, once the youth court has made a custody order, it leaves to the provincial director the administrative decision on the place and level of custody appropriate for the young offender.
The provincial director also has the flexibility to move offenders between institutions and programs and can authorize temporary releases to the community. In addition, the director can initiate an early release of a young person who is in custody to allow him or her to serve the balance of the disposition on probation in the community. Such a release is however, subject to review by the youth court at the request of the parties concerned.
It is the intent of the new act that the progress and welfare of young persons who receive custodial or other types of disposition should be subject to continuing attention and monitoring during the term of the disposition. To meet this objective, and to ensure that the public interest is safeguarded, an innovative and extensive review process is provided for, which will give all parties the opportunity not only to initiate the review of any dispositions but to attend and be heard. There will be a mandatory review in the case of any custodial disposition exceeding one year.

April 15, 1981
Young Offenders Act
Contrary to the Juvenile Delinquent's Act, which is silent on the matter, the new legislation contains provisions regulating the creation, maintenance, confidentiality and use of juvenile court records. Under the present legislation, it is possible for an individual to carry the label "delinquent" well beyond his youth and, indeed, possibly for life. Although young offenders are intended to take responsibility for their illegal behaviour, the consequences for them are not intended to be as severe as those applied to adults in the ordinary courts. Therefore, when a young offender has completed his or her sentence and committed no further offence for a qualifying period, the record will be destroyed. The young person will thus be given a fresh start when he or she has shown it is deserved. The effect of this provision is that there would in law be no conviction against the young person; he or she would not face all the disabilities that flow from having a criminal record. That provision, I feel, should provide a young person with a major incentive to mend his or her ways.
The final aspect of the new legislation which I wish to deal with and which is of major significance is that of the rights of young persons. In determining the responsibility of young persons under new legislation, it is to be recognized that young persons have particular rights and freedoms, including the right to be heard in the course of, and to participate in, the processes that lead to decisions that affect them, as well the opportunity to be informed of their right as guaranteed under the law.
The foregoing principle is representative of our belief that the full exercise of due process under the law should be extended to young persons. We can no longer operate under a system of procedural irregularity when a young person's freedom and liberty are at stake, nor should a young person be exposed to the sanctions of the criminal law without at the same time receiving the benefits of the built-in protections it has to offer. A young person must be given the opportunity to defend himself and be judged in accordance with the principles of natural justice. No longer can we dispense with such fundamental rights because they are seen to conflict with treatment and rehabilitation ideologies, nor allow the exercise of unfettered discretion in dealing with young persons. I believe that the goals of reformation and rehabilitation for children are compatible with the protection of procedural guarantees.
Under the proposed legislation, the young person would have the right to retain and instruct counsel at all stages of proceedings in which he is involved. Special safeguards would be established in order to assure proper and equitable practices in the taking of statements. Parents would be notified of any arrest, detention and court appearance respecting their child and granted the opportunity to participate in the proceedings. Rules of evidence and procedure would provide the opportunity to challenge the Crown's case and present a defence. Furthermore, young persons would be granted the same rights of appeal as are available to adults.
It must seem strange to those who are unfamiliar with the existing legislation which affects young persons to hear that these rights and procedures do not presently exist. I look forward very much to moving those particular aspects of the legislation forward. The proposed legislation, which has undergone many changes and modifications in response to the views and recommendations expressed through a lengthy consultation process, will bring us a significant step closer to the achievement of a desired equilibrium between the prime objective of the criminal law to protect the public from criminal behaviour and the desirability of ministering to the needs of young persons who come into conflict with the law.
Last summer I had the honour and privilege of leading the Canadian delegation attending the sixth United Nations congress on crime and treatment of offenders in Caracas, at which the subject of juvenile justice was an official agenda topic. I was greatly encouraged by the fact that the only resolution adopted on this subject was to the effect that standard minimum rules for the administration of juvenile justice should be developed so as to protect the fundamental rights of young persons. The specific principles agreed upon largely reflected those included in the proposed Young Offenders Act.
I must say I am equally gratified to see the solid support and encouragement extended to the government and myself by the press and others who have commented on the new legislation. I am hopeful, as I indicated at the outset, that the bill can be referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs for further examination at an early date, and I will do my utmost to prevent any unwarranted delays in the passage of this legislation, the realization of which is so crucial to the youth of the country.
I want to add a word about a study, which I authorized and is now under way, of the juvenile justice system. What I have in mind and what is being developed by the research division of my ministry is a study on the functioning of, the juvenile court to examine the activities undertaken by juvenile justice personnel in response to young persons being introduced to the juvenile justice system, observing the processing of juveniles in court, conducting surveys of court personnel and of parents and juveniles observed in the court. This is a study which will involve seven private research organizations in Vancouver, Edmonton, Winnipeg, Toronto, Montreal, Halifax, Kelowna, B.C., Granby, Cowansville and Saint-Hyacinthe. There will also be a research initiative directed toward the rural circuit outside of Edmonton.
What I have in mind and what this study, which will cover a period of years, will develop is an assessment of the efficiency and effectiveness of the juvenile justice system, in the hope that changes can be made to the administration and that there can be an assessment of the effectiveness of the legislation I am now presenting in its early years of operation. This would show whether there are ways that the system could be made more effective and efficient in order to achieve its goals and also to satisfy taxpayers that it is operating as effectively and efficiently as possible.
April 15, 1981

May I conclude by urging the House to refer this legislation to the justice committee, so that the views of experts can be added to those of Members of Parliament, the legislation can be given full consideration and brought into effect as expeditiously as possible.

speechtext: Why did your House leader agree?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
The minister asks why the House leader agreed. The minister phoned and asked me specifically while I was in a committee meeting yesterday about the timing of bringing this legislation forward. I do not want to dwell on this aspect too long. I just want to let the minister know how unhappy I am with the way in which he has conducted himself. I agreed to make some calls to see whether it would be appropriate to go ahead and accommodate the minister in his request, but before I got back to my office I was advised that the deal was already finalized. We were advised and informed unilaterally by the government House leader, without any suggestion that there was anything wrong with it, that this legislation would be brought forward today. I have said enough about it now; I do not want to waste any more time. I simply say that I am very unhappy with the way in which this matter has been dealt with. I just want to vent my spleen, if I may, on the minister at this point so I can deal with the merits of the legislation in a proper way.
I want to deal with the bill and some of the developments which have taken place in regard to it. As the minister has pointed out, the legislation which this bill is replacing, the Juvenile Delinquents Act, was adopted in 1908. It was passed as a result of a concerted campaign by several child care workers and magistrates who were inspired by the youth court movement in the United States and the social reform ideas in vogue at that time.
In 1929, the act was consolidated with amendments which revised it somewhat. That was as a result of a federal-provincial conference on the revision of the Juvenile Delinquents Act. Despite minor amendments made by Parliament in 1932, 1935, 1936, 1947, 1949, 1951, 1972 and 1979, the act is to all intents and purposes the same legislation as that which existed in 1929.
I want to draw to the attention of the House some of the main features of the legislation. The philosophy of the present Juvenile Delinquents Act is a parents patriae social welfare type of approach wherein juveniles are seen as not being responsible for their actions. Juvenile courts are given complete jurisdiction over a child who has committed a delinquency, which might consist of a violation of the Criminal Code, a federal-provincial statute, a bylaw or an ordinance of a munic-

April 15, 1981
Young Offenders Act
ipality, performance of immoral acts of some description or definition.
Under the present legislation, no formal diversion procedure exists whereby a young person is sent to a social agency rather than being processed by the court. Under the present legislation, if a young person has committed a delinquency, a judge can impose sanctions alone or in combination with such things as a fine of up to $25, placement on probation or placement in a foster home. There is provision for committal to the care of the Children's Aid Society or committal to a training school as well as the possibility of imposition of other conditions, such as restitution or the performance of a community service.
It may be important for us to understand what has led up to this particular legislation. There has been a considerable amount of consultation and study. A number of publications and reports have been prepared and issued on the problem of juvenile delinquents. In 1961, the then minister of justice established a five-man departmental committee on juvenile delinquents. In 1966, the standing committee in this House reported on juvenile delinquency and the report was tabled in the House. In 1968, a federal-provincial conference of justice ministers was held. They discussed the justice committee report and the reform of the juvenile justice system. In 1970, legislation was introduced through Bill C-192 in that year; it was called the young offenders act. It received first reading but was allowed to die because of some severe criticism levelled at the legislation during the course of that year.
In 1973, a federal-provincial conference of corrections ministers was held. They established a federal-provincial review group on the juvenile justice system. Also in that year, the solicitor general at the time set up an interdepartmental committee on young persons in conflict with the law. In 1975, that committee submitted its report. Between 1975 and 1977, the solicitor general's department initiated a consultative process on the 1975 committee report. In 1977, the solicitor general tabled a document called "Highlights of the Proposed New Legislation for Young Offenders". In June 1977, a federal-provincial conference of attorneys general and ministers of corrections discussed the highlights of the proposals. In 1979, the parliamentary secretary to the then solicitor general tabled the document entitled "Legislative Proposals to Replace the Juvenile Delinquents Act".
The present state of affairs in Canada is simply this. The juvenile justice problem is a significant one. In 1978, there were close to 91,000 delinquencies processed under the existing act. It is widely recognized that the law as it presently stands is outmoded and ineffective. It is badly in need of modernization. The preceding administration of the Progressive Conservative government had undertaken to make significant changes in the law, as evidenced in the document tabled in the fall of 1979 to which I have just referred.
To the extent this bill, C-61, is a manifestation of a realization that the law is in need of change, it is welcomed literally by everyone in the justice field. Many studies and reports that have been done in recent years indicate clearly there is need for change.
I want to look briefly at some of the provisions of the bill and consider the consequences and changes that are affected by this legislation. First, in terms of the policy approach of the bill, the minister made reference to the basic premise and philosophy of the bill in his opening remarks today. He referred to the three principles of the legislation. First, that young people should be held more responsible, although not wholly or fully accountable, with respect to their activities; second, that society does have a right to protection; third, that the young offender does have a right to due process and fair treatment.
The philosophy of the existing legislation respecting juvenile delinquents is found in Section 3(2). It provides that a child shall be dealt with "not as an offender, but as one in a condition of delinquency and therefore requiring help and guidance and proper supervision." If members refer to the paper tabled in this House in October 1975, they will see that the provision in the bill is similar to those set forth on pages 2 and 3 of the legislative proposals tabled by the then solicitor general.
Second, with regard to offences covered by jurisdiction, this bill covers only specific offences against the Criminal Code and other federal statutes and regulations. The offence of delinquency under the present law is abolished; the minister made reference to that. I will return to that aspect of the bill because there are some areas in which intensive negotiations and discussions with provincial counterparts will be absolutely essential to ensure that the legislation is fully effective. Without the assistrance and co-operation of the provincial authorities, the legislation will not be effective. In fact, it will suffer some very serious defects.
The position with respect to restricting the application of this legislation to the federal area of jurisdiction is in keeping with the recommendation made by the Law Reform Commission. It suggested excluding less serious conduct from the ambit of criminal law. I again refer hon. members to the 1979 report, page 4.
The third aspect is the way in which this bill deals with jurisdiction by age. The minister pointed out that the age of criminal responsibility has been raised from seven to 12 years of age. The maximum age will be 18 years. However, at the request of a province, the government may set the age of under 16 or 17 as the maximum in a particular province. The present legislation sets the maximum age at under 16, but allows for the establishment of different maximum ages upon provincial request.
This provision is quite interesting to me. I will refer to that later as well. It is an arbitrary age. There are some difficulties in terms of legislation affecting people on the basis of age. There are different people involved, different levels of maturity and development and different circumstances. I am sure everyone here will agree with the increase in the age to which this legislation would apply. As the minister stated, there have been consultations with the provinces. Two provinces suggest-
April 15, 1981

ed that the minimum age be raised to 14. The remaining provinces, the majority of those consulted, were satisfied with age 12. Statistics show that a significant number of 12 and 13 year olds are in conflict with the law. We should look at this revision if there is some area of complaint with respect to the way in which these particular provisions are going to apply in relation to uniformity of law across Canada.
In our debate recently on the Constitution, the government introduced the concept of opting out. Yet this is a very undesirable trait in legislation, according to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and other spokesmen for the government, including the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien). We have to ask ourselves whether this kind of provision will provide for the so-called checkerboard effect across Canada. For example, a young person may commit a criminal offence on the Mac-donald-Cartier bridge which crosses the Ottawa river between Ontario and Quebec. At which end of the bridge the offence is committed will have some bearing. At one end of the bridge, if charged, he can take advantage of the Young Offenders Act, whereas if it occurs at the other end in the other province, it is quite a different proposition. One province may have determined the appropriate maximum age is 16, whereas in the other jurisdiction it may be under 18. I do not know where that would lead. Young offenders may decide to move to a jurisdiction where they can take advantage of a more modern law.
In terms of principles of criminal law and the uniformity concept, we should look at bringing some uniformity to this provision. It has been suggested by such people as the distinguished member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid) that during the course of committee meetings we provide an option to those under the age of 18 years to make application in an adult court to have the young offenders provisions apply. In other words, young people across Canada could have available to them the provisions of this act even though the age of majority varies from province to province.
Suggestions will be made in committee in the hope we can come to some conclusion. I take it from the remarks of the Solicitor General there will be full and thorough examination in committee. There will be an opportunity to consult broadly with the people involved, young offenders and other young people, counsellors and others involved in pilot projects across Canada. The committee should have the advantage of that kind of testimony and full opportunity to ensure that the legislation will be the most effective that we can pass in this House. That is certainly the intent of members of my party, and I trust of all members of the House.
I want to deal with another aspect of the bill with regard to the diversion provisions. The bill makes special provision for diversions. Not all young persons who break federal laws have to appear in the youth court. Under this legislation, in lieu of having a case tried before the court, they have the option of providing a community service or agreeing to make restitution to the victim. This is all voluntary. It is an interesting and novel provision which I believe will receive general support.
Young Offenders Act
There is nothing in the bill to preclude the accused from having the right to have the matter tried in the young offenders court where guilt or innocence can be established. Under the present legislation, there is no provision for a formal diversion procedure. There are provisions which have a similar effect in that a judge may have a hearing and then provide that the matter be adjourned sine die, to a date in the future not specified, without having guilt established if the accused agrees to some type of rehabilitative program. While there has been the development of this kind of practice in the courts, this new legislation will give formal recognition to the ability of the court to allow the accused young offender to perform a community service or make restitution without the necessity of fighting the case. It seems to me it has been recognized for some time that the criminal law need not be invoked in all circumstances. Many young people are needlessly appearing in juvenile courts.
I want to turn now to the nature of proceedings under this particular legislation. The bill is said to establish strong guidelines for proceedings. Offenders rights are made explicit; there is a right to counsel at all stages of the proceedings and a judge is required under this legislation to advise young people of their rights. This is different from the present act which is silent on rights. It provides that under summary conviction procedures the provisions of the Criminal Code apply. It also provides that all trials shall be as informal as possible. We will want to look at these provisions to make sure the rights and interests of not only the alleged young offender but also of society as a whole are adequately protected. We are entering new ground, uncharted waters, in this area.
The fifth aspect I should like to deal with has regard to the provisions in respect of detention and bail. The bill gives the same entitlement to bail as exists for adult offenders at the present time. The legislation does contain provisions by which notice must be given to a young person's parents, and provisions under which a young offender will by and large, in every case possible, be detained separately from adult offenders. The bill does provide that a young offender can be placed in the hands of a responsible adult to avoid the strict custody contemplated by incarceration in an institution.
The sixth aspect deals with transfer to adult court. This bill would allow such transfer when an offence is committed by a young offender after his fourteenth birthday. There are explicit criteria provided to guide a judge's decision. A judge must consider the so-called predisposition report and the parents' representations before making a transfer order, and transfer orders in themselves are subject to appeal. Again this is another area we will want to look at very closely, particularly the criteria judges must consider when making an order, to make sure the rights of young offenders and society are adequately and properly protected.
The seventh aspect is in respect of disposition. The minister has referred to disposition, known otherwise as sentencing powers. There is a wide range of options, anywhere from

April 15, 1981
Young Offenders Act
absolute discharge to incarceration for up to two years, with a wide range of additional conditions which a judge may feel appropriate under the circumstances.
Other aspects of the bill which are dealt with are fingerprinting and photographs. The bill does provide for photographs and fingerprints to be taken, but these are to be destroyed if there is an acquittal or if the proceedings are discontinued. There are also special provisions in respect of storage of these kinds of records, with control of access to the information in respect of young offenders. The present act is silent with regard to the authority to take photographs and fingerprints. This issue has been the subject of conflicting judicial determination in the recent past, so these provisions will be helpful in clarifying a situation which is now unclear, at least on the basis of judicial interpretation.
The bill does provide for public hearings. As members of the House know, juvenile delinquency matters have by and large been carried on in camera, away from public scrutiny. At the present time there is a prohibition against publication in the press particularly of names mentioned in the deliberations before a juvenile court. Under this bill the courtroom will be open, but restrictions remain on press reports regarding trials in juvenile courts.
The philosophy under the present act was that trials of children should take place without publicity and separately and apart from the trials of other accused persons. Everyone will agree that in camera hearings should be, and generally are, viewed with some suspicion and are more susceptible to potential abuse. As long as protection is afforded the young offender, with a prohibition against the publication of names and identifying information in relation to the young offender, it may be a step forward in opening the whole process of allowing more access to these courts, placing the court, its officers and even the judiciary under public scrutiny.
I will conclude my comments by dealing with some of the principles of the bill. With regard to youth court records under this legislation, when a sentence is completed and no further offence is committed within a qualifying period the records will be destroyed. The qualifying period is two years for a summary conviction and five years for an indictable conviction.
In the present situation there is no provision for the destruction of records, and there are no regulations for the creation and maintenance of confidentiality of, or accessibility to, juvenile records. Indeed, a young person after conviction could be labelled a delinquent for life under the law as it now exists. That situation will be changed by these provisions. As I say, there can be no argument against the proposition that young persons should be responsible for their actions, but one would hope that these illegal acts carried out by people in their youth should not carry severely undue consequences. One thing hoped to be accomplished by this legislation is that young people will be given an opportunity to make a fresh start in life through rehabilitation and redemption.
I think it fair to imply in general terms that our party agrees
with the concept contained in this legislation. It is in fact
modelled very much on the legislation brought forward by my colleague, the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland, when he was solicitor general. I recall that the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland said when this legislation was tabled he would grade it in terms of the three Rs. He said the bill does in fact give greater responsibility, does in fact provide for greater rights in respect of young offenders and does provide for greater flexibility in rehabilitation.
As I said at the outset, I do not know why the Solicitor General had to wait for the one day in the whole year when the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland was out of the House to bring forward this legislation. That hon. member may have been away another day because of illness, but I believe this is only the second day he has been absent. He is a faithful attendant. The fact of the matter is that the matter has been before him for some considerable time. He has indicated there are some provisions which must be looked at in terms of our committee work. It is very important for us to see that we obtain the best possible legislation, and I have addressed myself to some of its aspects. Obviously this bill cannot be the whole or total solution to the problem. It can only treat the symptoms of the disease. Young people in our country in their formative years need to be given some alternative to being on the streets and facing very severe criminal consequences.
There are some statistics which are quite distressing in terms of the development of criminal records and in terms of criminal activities in our country. Between 80 per cent and 90 per cent of adult criminals in Canada had their first brush with the law as juveniles. In such places as Winnipeg, Manitoba authorities have been in contact with more than 10,000 juveniles with respect to a variety of delinquencies ranging from highway traffic infractions to murder. The investigation to which I am referring revealed that boys as young as 15 years of age were charged with attempted murder and rape last year. In 1980, ten-year-old males were turned over to juvenile authorities to face charges of indecent assault and wounding. Boys of eight were charged with robbery.
As we sit in our comfortable pews across the country, we sometimes do not realize that these kinds of offences are occurring. I once came home to my own house and found that a magnificent robbery had taken place there. There was hardly a trace of the robbers. There was a broken window under a porch. It was a very professional job. I saw a couple of leaves on the floor. The perpetrators had gone upstairs without disturbing a thing and had taken a collection of silver coins. I was just amazed at that time to find that the robbers were two eight-year-olds. They were caught because a confectioner in the district became suspicious when he saw those silver coins. He called the police, who apprehended the boys. I happened to be talking to the juvenile court judge the next day. I told him how surprised I was to see these young children involved in this theft. It was hard for me to believe. He said, "This is the third time they have been before me". They each were eight years old.
April 15, 1981

This shows that some new approach has to be taken with respect to allowing such children opportunities for another new chance. This legislation by itself will not solve all these problems, but let us hope it is some assistance in terms of creating a slightly different attitude toward juvenile offenders.
Of course, certain young offenders are not covered by this legislation. They will be dealt with by social welfare officials, which gives rise to a conundrum. We are raising the age to 12 years, and everyone agrees that that is good, but whether social welfare agencies in each of the provinces will be able to deal adequately with this kind of situation is another problem.
I think we should look at these things in committee and try to determine what is best for our young people and for society.
On February 14, 1981 the Winnipeg Free Press reported on an interview given by Sister Geraldine MacNamara, the director of the Rossbrook House, which will be known to hon. members from Winnipeg. Sister Geraldine spoke about young people getting into conflicts with the law at early ages. In the article Sister Geraldine said:
"If you have children getting into conflict with the law at a very early age it seems there are several other factors at work besides simple moral depravity-"
The article went on to say:
These young people are dealt with by professionals briefly or taken care of for a year or two in an institution and are then "immediately thrown right back into the same situation they came from," she said.
They must be given alternatives to a life on the street.
"As long as neighborhoods are allowed to deteriorate and people are left in a virtually hopeless situation, social problems like young offenders will continue," she said.
I suppose people such as the good sister who deal with these problems have an understanding of some of the problems we face in society with respect to dealing with young offenders and the very serious difficulties we have in trying to create an atmosphere in which these young people can have the opportunity in life so many of us have enjoyed in our great country, with its terrific potential and the opportunities which are available. If opportunities are available for so many, they should be available for all.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Hear, hear!
