speechtext:
In this context I want also to make reference to the vital importance of working in conjunction with the provinces. Because if this legislation is passed in its present form, children under the age of 12 will no longer be covered under any provisions of the Juvenile Delinquents Act or the proposed young offenders act. Violations of provincial and municipal law will no longer be covered under the legislation, so the provinces need time and should be given time to develop appropriate complementary legislation.
An interview with Ross Paisley, the deputy attorney general of the province of Alberta, was reported in The Calgary Herald on February 18, 1981. In that interview Mr. Paisley said, and I quote:
"We've been working on this-
That is, complementary legislation to the proposed young offenders act.
Young Offenders Act
-for some time and now just hope that we have enough lead time to get it into place"-
The article went on to say:
The proposed act does not cover offences under provincial and municipal laws. The province, Paisley said, must therefore develop complementary legislation to deal with provincial and municipal offences.
He also made reference to the fact that his department will have to examine the child welfare act in that province to see if it needs beefing up in its provisions for children under the age of 12 years. This indicates that each of the provincial jurisdictions will now be directly affected by this legislation since it will put a new onus and a new responsibility on the provinces to deal with the void which now exists because of the changes brought about by this legislation.
In view of the fact that the federal government is taking this initiative, it is absolutely essential that there be full co-operation with provincial authorities to make sure there is, if at all possible, the most uniform treatment of our young people in Canada. It is one thing for the federal government to take steps which would reduce its responsibility under this act; it is another thing to do it only after such time as it is satisfied that there is adequate provision made for young people under the age of 12.
My colleague, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), has pointed out to me that there has been some work done with respect to a diversion program in his city of St. John's. He indicates to me that it is an extremely impressive pilot project. He points out that the program secretariat was established in May of 1979. In September of 1979, the program received its first cases. Since that time more than 350 juveniles have paticipated in this pre-charge program which has brought both offender and victim together to work out a suitable settlement. Twenty-three volunteer mediators underwent training for their work, and these 23 volunteer mediators have been involved in mediation sessions, which have attempted to focus the responsibility on the offender. I think this is one of the purposes of this legislation.
My colleague has also brought to my attention some research work which has been done by a Dr. Frechette, who has been conducting research on juvenile offenders within the juvenile court system of Montreal. Dr. Frechette's early findings leave no doubt that the expansion of diversion programs, self-help programs and so forth is urgently needed across this country. Thus far, Dr. Frechette has studied 400 juvenile offenders. Of those 400 cases, 50 per cent have already made adult court appearances. Of those 200 individuals, between 70 and 80 have been sentenced to terms in penitentiaries. The question is and remains, how many of those 200 individuals might have been spared appearances in court in their adult years if programs such as diversion had been in operation?
We in this party are prepared to deal in a responsible manner with this legislation. I trust the legislation will be dealt with fairly and expeditiously. I hope it will be before the committee as soon as the committee has completed its work on

April 15, 1981
Voung Offenders Act
the freedom of information legislation, which I hope will be completed before too long.
We compliment the Solicitor General for following the initiative which was taken by the previous solicitor general, the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland. In his very brief period of time, he was an outstanding solicitor general. We hope the current Solicitor General will follow the traditions established by my colleague.
We accept the principle of this legislation, we want to work on it in committee, and I thank the House for its indulgence in allowing me to address this important piece of legislation.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to participate in this debate on what is undoubtedly one of the most important bills which has come before this session of the House of Commons. As the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) indicated, we are dealing with legislation which has essentially been unamended and unchanged in substance since 1908 when it was originally introduced. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) points out that that was the year of his birth; of course, it was a very good year indeed.
In examining the provisions of this bill, it is important to look back at some of the principles which have guided legislators and parliamentarians in the past and which society has applied generally in dealing with the problem of young offenders or young people in society who have violated the law. There have been many attitudes taken to young offenders. Some
2,000	years ago, Socrates wrote:
Our youths now love luxury, they have had manners, they have disrespect for authority, disrespect for older people. Children generally are tyrants. They no longer rise when adults enter the room ... They gobble food and tyrannize their teachers.
That was not the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre speaking about the hon. member for Burnaby; that was what Socrates wrote some 2,000 years ago.
The response to various forms of inappropriate conduct on the part of young people has also varied over the course of history. We have seen very, very harsh measures taken against young people, measures which would be unthinkable today. For example, during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, the use of hanging was commonplace in cases of serious offences by children, some as young as seven or eight years old. One example is an English case at Abingdon Assizes before Whitlock. One John Dean, an infant eight years old, was indicted, arraigned and found guilty of burning two barns in the town of Windsor. It appearing upon examination that he had malice, revenge, craft and cunning, he had judgment to be hanged and was hanged accordingly. That is how they dealt in those days with persons who burned barns. We might contrast that with the response of the present day.
As I said, the legislation was initially enacted in 1908. It was principled upon progressive reforms. The tone and purpose of that legislation was not to treat young persons as criminals, but to quote from the legislation itself, as "a misdirected and
misguided child"; one needing "aid, encouragement, help and assistance".
There is no question that the Juvenile Delinquents Act of 1908 is seriously outdated today and must be substantially changed. But we must be very careful, in amending and overhauling this important piece of legislation, to keep in mind the important principle which was enunciated in the 1908 legislation, that we must not replace this bill with a Criminal Code for children. We must bear in mind the fact that young people who come in contact with the law must be dealt with in a special manner and that adequate resources must be brought to bear to deal with them.
It has been suggested by the drafters of the legislation that there is a shift in emphasis away from the important principle of 1908. In fact, one policy analyst of the Department of the Solicitor General, Mr. Tom Sterritt, has been very actively involved in drafting the bill. He stated that the new bill changes the focus of the law and that it may not be the needs or the welfare of the child that are paramount any more; it may be the protection of society. Indeed, the protection of society is and must be of great importance, but one must question whether by substituting a Criminal Code for children we in any way enhance the protection of society. I suggest the evidence is very much to the contrary.
Many studies have been done in the past of this important area, starting back in 1965 when a committee of the Department of Justice examined the area. In 1970, a bill was proposed in the House which met with great resistance and was substantially withdrawn by the government. In 1975, the interdepartmental committee tabled a report entitled "Young Persons in Conflict with the Law", which made a number of important and progressive recommendations. I will come back to that report in a few minutes. In 1977, there was a further attempt by the then solicitor general to bring in a document known as "Highlights of the Proposed Young Offenders Legislation", which withdrew from some of the important principles suggested in the 1975 report. Finally, as was mentioned earlier, in 1979 the Conservative government tabled a document indicating the general nature of the legislation they would be proposing in this important area.
There is no question that there are serious deficiencies in this area of the law, in the area of how we as a society deal with young people who have violated the law. Those deficiencies in the legislative structure have led to great frustration on the part of all people affected by them, starting, of course, with the police, who must enforce what is recognized by many to be a totally inadequate law. In many cases the police know that the resources which are being availed to young offenders are completely inadequate. Unfortunately-and I say this in the case of some police officers-their response is one of violence. They believe the young person will not be adequately dealt with within the context of the criminal justice system, and, therefore, in some cases we see instances of brutality against young people who have come in conflict with the law.
Fortunately this is not a common occurrence, but the recent
report of a respected group in the province of Ontario, Justice
April 15, 1981

for Children, documented a number of serious concerns in this area. I point this out as evidence of the fact that the police forces of the country are as frustrated as other elements in the justice community with the inadequacies of the Juvenile Delinquents Act as it presently stands.
There are suggestions of excessive force being used during arrests. There are suggestions of harassment of young people who have come in conflict with the law following their return to their communities. Surely these kinds of things must not be condoned. Hopefully they will be dealt with, not only through changes in legislation, but through changes in resources.
We must also recognize the concern of members of the judiciary. Juvenile court judges have commented frequently on the inadequacies of the Juvenile Delinquents Act and in many cases have expressed their exasperation and despair at the lack of an adequate judicial framework and a lack of resources. I will deal with the question of resources later in the course of my remarks.
We must recognize the element in the judicial equation which is often forgotten, and that is the victim of the offence. Too often we forget about the fact that there is a victim. The victim is shunted to one side, is not informed of what is taking place as a result of the offence, and of course suffers and feels quite justifiably that he is not an important element in the disposition of the offence.
We must bear in mind that there should be adequate victim support mechanisms. I am pleased to note that the Department of the Solicitor General has a couple of pilot studies presently under way which are attempting to focus greater attention on the role of the victim, with follow-up mechanisms to ensure that the victim is not a forgotten member of the justice community in cases such as this.
It goes without saying that in too many instances young people themselves who have violated the law hold those very laws in contempt. In many cases they recognize that they are dealing with the judicial treadmill and that the treadmill is one which is completely unsatisfactory to deal with the very serious concerns which society must face in the area of violations of the law, both in terms of violations of property law and in terms of the increased incidence of violence against persons, such as, for example, assaults. So, this is an important area. It must be dealt with. We must recognize that all elements of the justice community, whether it be the judiciary, probation officers-whom I have not mentioned yet but who are dealing with excessive case loads in many cases-the young people themselves and the police, all say that the time has come to fundamentally overhaul the way in which we deal with young offenders.
What about this legislation? There certainly are a number of welcome provisions in it, provisions which are long overdue. For example, the end to status offences and the hodge-podge of offences which in this day and age must surely no longer be contained in a civilized Juvenile Delinquents Act.
Young Offenders Act
Another such provision is the omnibus charge of juvenile delinquency, which includes sexual immorality or any similar form of vice, whatever that means. We have seen that this is a particularly invidious provision because it often discriminates on the basis of sex. Young female delinquents are much more liable to be charged under this particular provision than are young male delinquents. Statistics for the most recent years show that while 11 per cent of all young people who were charged with delinquency were females, 42 per cent of those young persons who were charged with this particular offence of sexual immorality were females. In many ways it is a crime of female delinquency. We welcome the fact that this will be abolished in the new legislation.
We welcome the provision for public trials. We support the suggestion that while trials should be public, the names of the young people accused should not be disclosed. We welcome the end to indeterminate sentencing which, once again, constitutes discrimination against young people. At the present time no adult is subject to this form of indeterminate sentencing and surely, as a matter of equality before the law, this kind of sentencing should not exist. We,are pleased to note that the new legislation would accept the recommendations of a number of committees and put an end to indeterminate sentencing.
We note that there are guidelines on the transfer of young offenders to adult court. At the present time the Juvenile Delinquents Act contains no guidelines. We recognize that the explicit mention of guidelines is long overdue in suggesting to the judiciary that when they exercise their discretion it must be exercised with extreme care. We may be soliciting the views of a number of witnesses as to whether or not the age of 14 is an adequate one and should be maintained for transfer or whether that age should be raised, as the Committee of Young Persons in Conflict with the Law suggested. They suggested that it should be raised to 16 years of age.
We welcome the increase in the age of criminal responsibility from seven years of age to 12. There are arguments which have been made, and we certainly will be examining them with care, to the effect that the minimum age of criminal responsibility should be increased beyond 12 years of age and that it should go as high as 13, or 14, as is the case in the Province of Quebec. Those arguments are compelling arguments, Mr. Speaker. In fact, they were accepted by the very distinguished committee which produced the report, namely, the committee of young persons in conflict with the law. I would suggest that there must be very strong reasons for rejecting that particular recommendation.
Finally, we are pleased to note the long overdue implementation of procedural safeguards, the right to access to legal counsel, the right to bail, and a number of other important procedural safeguards which so far have been denied young people who have come before the juvenile courts, although we might say that a number of judges have voluntarily extended those provisions in their courts. I would note that it was a Juvenile Court judge from the province of Alberta, the very distinguished Judge Litsky, who described the procedures in

April 15, 1981
Young Offenders Act
juvenile court as being star chamber procedures or black magic courtrooms. As I said, we welcome an end to those particular provisions of the Juvenile Delinquents Act. We welcome the recognition that young people are entitled to the same procedural safeguards as adults, since in many cases they are subject to very serious penalties if they are found guilty.
Having pointed out our support for these provisions in the proposed bill, and frankly, a number of other provisions in the bill, we do have serious concerns which we believe must be addressed. If there is one concern which is greater than all the rest, and which surely represents a flagrant violation of the principle of equality before the law, and which represents, in my view, a violation of the government's own charter of fundamental rights and freedoms, it is the government's failure to bite the bullet and impose a standard age, a standard maximum age right across this land to define what constitutes a young offender. The government has copped out on this important question and its excuses are simply not adequate.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: They have opted out.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
As the hon. member suggests, they have opted out. Of course, what this does is to create a checkerboard of rights right across this land. We have heard that from the Conservative Party because, of course, they have proposed an amending formula which would permit this very checkerboard of rights right across Canada. The hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) has recently suggested that maybe that is not what they will be doing, and the hon. member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn) shakes his head quizzically. We are not exactly sure where he stands on this important question of a checkerboard of rights or a floor of rights right across the land. It can surely not be suggested that to define a young person in the city of Ottawa as a criminal and put him into the adult justice system and into an adult penitentiary for exactly the same conduct which a young person in Hull, across the Ottawa River, would be defined a juvenile delinquent, a young offender, and would be given the additional resources and would have been kept out of that adult penal system, is the right way to go about things. So, many of us here recognize that the penal system is almost an admission of failure, because if a young person of 16 or 17 years of age enters into such a system, there is no doubt whatsoever that their chances of getting out are very slim indeed. There have been many groups who have recommended-indeed, insisted-that there must be a simple recognition of equality before the law, a standard upper maximum age. The committee of young persons in conflict with the law in its report considered various options and recommended that the youth court have exclusive jurisdiction to deal with young persons between the ages of 14 and 18 years of age who have committed an offence. That committee has accepted as an absolutely essential requirement that there must be a standard maximum age right across the country.
I have said that the government's actions violate its own charter of rights. Section 15 of that charter says there can be no discrimination on the basis of age. How else can this
particular provision of the Young Offenders Act be construed than as discriminating on the basis of age or as denying equal benefit before the law? I predict that if the government is foolish enough to go ahead with this provision, it will be challenged very quickly in the courts of our land where it will be thrown out as a violation of the government's own charter of rights. Thus, Mr. Speaker, that provision must be changed.
We welcome the suggestion that young people should be diverted from the formal criminal justice process wherever possible. But there are very grave dangers in the absence of any kind of adequate guidelines for dealing with diversion in this proposed bill. There are just simply not sufficient safeguards.
The concern here, of course, is one which has been echoed by a number of persons. Once again the excellent report of the committee of young persons in conflict with the law recommended a form of mandatory screening, a suggestion which is presently in effect in the province of Quebec. The Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) suggested that he was not prepared to accept that, because there must be an opportunity for a young person to plead not guilty. Of course, that could be a part of this legislation, and naturally should be a part of this legislation. We recognize that there is a very real danger in opfcning up the possibility of diversion. If adequate safeguards are not applied, the police and the prosecutors will, in some cases, use forms of coercion. When they do not have what they consider to be a safe enough case or a tight enough case legally, they might attempt to divert a young offender who, had he gone to court, would have been acquitted of a particular offence. So we must examine very carefully the diversion provisions. I suggest we must consider very favourably the possibility of a form of mandatory screening. We will want to hear from a number of witnesses on this particular suggestion.
The bill suggests that young people should be separated from adults when they are being detained. I am sure everyone in this House would agree with that principle. However, it permits a cop-out again, because what the bill says is that young people must be detained separately from adults, but when there is no place of detention for young persons available within a reasonable distance, they can be detained with adults. Not only does that violate the provisions of the international covenant on civil and political rights, but surely it must violate all standards of criminal justice which this House is prepared to accept.
To suggest that a young person, 14 or 15 years of age, could be detained pending trial with adults, with people who in many cases have been convicted of a number of offences, surely cannot be condoned. It is happening today. I can give a couple of examples. In the province of Quebec, a 15-year-old boy was kept in an adult jail. Why was he kept in an adult jail? Because there was no facility in Quebec to deal with anglophone juveniles. Nine out of 15 anglophone juveniles last year in the province of Quebec were sent to adult prisons. There is, as the social affairs minister in Quebec admitted himself, a
April 15, 1981

chronic need for a centre dealing exclusively with anglophones. Of course, this bill would perpetrate that kind of inequity.
We see that in the city of Saint John, New Brunswick, there are young people who are being detained in cells in the same jail as adults. Of course, they are kept in separate cells, but, once again, this is not a separate facility. These children are being kept in a jail with adults. That must not be tolerated and the bill must be changed in that respect.
We have concerns about the provisions with respect to the subsequent use of records from youth court proceedings. There can be an argument made that a judge who is considering sentencing or disposition should have access to the full history of the person before him or her. However, to suggest that this record can be used more generally is, I would submit, a suggestion which could give rise to abuse. We will want to hear again from witnesses on that.
These are some of our concerns about the bill, but I suggest one of the most important concerns which must be addressed in this area of young offenders in the law is the whole question of prevention. This is an area which, with respect, neither of the two previous speakers have addressed. One need only look at the recent report which was tabled by the standing Senate committee on health, welfare and science, an outstanding repcft, entitled "Child at Risk". It points out that we, as a society, have failed our children, that those children who are being processed through the criminal justice system in many cases have no business being there, had we taken adequate preventive steps. It identifies a number of measures which could be taken, and points out that in many cases the failure to take these steps results not only in a young person coming in conflict with the law at the juvenile stage, but results as well in further criminal activity and in a budget of over $.5 billion for our correctional system in this country.
What are some of the factors that this committee identified? Surprising as it may be to some, perhaps, it said that we must go right back to the prenatal stage. We must look at malnutrition of the pregnant mother. We must look at the whole question of intrauterine abuse, the fetal alcohol syndrome, for example, the effect of smoking, the effect of the use of some drugs on the fetus itself. We must look at the effects of prenatal emotional stress. We must look, as well, of course, even after the child is born, at diet and at possible metabolic disorders. I suggest there should be some form of mandatory screening of all young people to ensure that they do not have dietary deficiencies or metabolic disorders. So, it pinpoints the prenatal stage as being one important area.
It turns then to the paranatal stage and suggests that conditions at birth can influence the subsequent behaviour of the child. For example, it even points to the special care which must be taken with premature children. It then turns to the time-frame of early parenthood and points out that there are significant stresses on single parents, partly because of the inadequate resources which are available to these families in our society at present.
It talks about the effects of emotional deprivation. Study after study has shown that almost without exception, violent
Young Offenders Act
offenders have been shuffled between foster homes, have come from broken homes and have simply not had adequate resources when they were young. To quote from one study, they were unwanted at birth, they had frequent placements in infancy, and then graduated almost always from minor offences to major crimes.
The whole area of child abuse is another one which has been identified as an important element in dealing with the question of young offenders: the use of violence against children and the possibility that, in turn, children will see violence as an acceptable alternative. The distinction between a spanking and a beating, and the condonation of that distinction in our criminal code under Section 43, is one which I, for one, cannot support.
There are a number of other recommendations which are made by this excellent study and which I hope will be acted upon by the government. It talks about the influence of violence in the home and about the importance of parents and other role models in the home setting an example on the use of violence. Perhaps one of the most important areas that it pinpoints is the question of violence on television, the fact that in many cases television sets are used as babysitters, that in the course of an average child's lifetime, he or she will see on television some 13,000 or 14,000 people dying; the perpetration of values on television program after television program which suggest that the accumulation of wealth and greed is desirable; the despair and the frustration at the gap between expectation and reality. Violence unquestionably breeds violence. It points out the importance of adequate, well-funded daycare facilities to ensure that when a parent must work, the children are adequately looked after. We certainly support that recommendation.
Finally, it talks about the unquestionable link between poverty, about the fact that there are over one million children in this country who live in conditions of poverty, and the link between poverty and later juvenile delinquency. Let me quote the following from a report which is as valid today as it was when it was written in 1975, a report called "Poor Kids", by the National Council of Welfare:
To be born poor is to face a greater likelihood of ill health-in infancy, in childhood and throughout your adult life. To be born poor is to face a lesser likelihood that you will finish high school; lesser still that you will attend university. To be born poor is to face a greater likelihood that you will be judged a delinquent in adolescence and, if so, a greater likelihood that you will be sent to a 'correctional institution'. To be born poor is to have the deck stacked against you at birth, to find life an uphill struggle ever after. To be born poor is unfair to kids.
Surely, to be born poor, must be unacceptable to all members of this House.
What are some of the other concerns that must face us when dealing with this area of young people in conflict of the law? What is perhaps one of the most important concerns is the totally inadequate allocation of resources by governments, federal and provincial, to this important area. I need only point to an example in my own province. Recently a report was issued showing that juvenile offenders were being kept in overcrowded centres in British Columbia and that perhaps as

April 15, 1981
Young Offenders Act
many as 40 per cent or 50 per cent of the kids presently being held in detention centres have no business being there. The only reason they are there is because society has not provided the funds for any other resource. These youth detention centres, one of which is located in my constituency, are grossly overcrowded. There are no facilities whatsoever to deal with the psychiatrically disturbed young offender.
Where are our priorities as a nation when we can put millions and millions of dollars into building new penitentiaries in Renous and Dona Conna but fail to allocate adequate resources to ensure that young people who come in conflict with the law, are dealt with.
There are other concerns, Mr. Speaker. I have mentioned the example of the youth detention centres and the failure to allocate adequate resources to them. Many examples can be given of what we set as the priorities of this nation. I know that my time is limited and I will not abuse that, but I should like to give a couple more examples, if I may.
There are no secure psychiatric facilities whatsoever for juveniles in the province of British Columbia. Emotionally-ill children are mixed in with juvenile delinquents. The supervisor of one of the youth detention centres has said that all they can do is to assign staff to watch over disturbed youths. He said it was a really tough time for the staff because they feel so helpless and that "We just followed her around" referring to a particular patient.
In an article in the Vancouver Sun of March 6, 1980, a Dr. Gossage is quoted as follows:
I am unaware ... of any facility in this province which can help him. And I have to say I think that't just terrible.
... He is but one of many children who are going down the tube because of the failure of society to address this problem.
This is a scenario which is repeated in province after province. In Ottawa, the hospital has stopped admitting young people who are psychiatrically disturbed saying that unquestionably, unless the provincial government of Ontario allocates adequate resources, there will be suicides and serious repercussions as a result.
I could cite examples on and on, Mr. Speaker. What is clear is that our society has not placed adequate priority on the allocation of resources to young people who have come in conflict with the law. We have seen a dramatic increase in the suicide rate among young people. In the province of British Columbia, for example, 50 adolescents committed suicide in 1979. The failure to provide adequate treatment for emotionally disturbed young people is an indictment both of provincial and federal governments and is not dealt with by this bill. There must be adequate minimum standards right across this land.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, while I welcome a number of the innovations in this bill and recognize that some important steps forward are being taken, I have serious concerns over and above the concern with the bill itself. I suggest that we as a society must realign our priorities and recognize that our young people, our children, must be a priority. We must implement the recommendations of the committee on the
International Year of the Child and of the special Senate committee which wrote the report "Child at Risk". We must surely consult with these and other groups and with the provincial governments which must implement this legislation. I suggest we invite representatives of all provincial governments to appear before the justice committee as an example of the co-operation which should take place in this field.
If we can allocate millions and millions of dollars to the Space shuttle "Columbia" and take great pride in our accomplishments in that area, surely to goodness the time has come to allocate adequate resources to young people in this country.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank you for the opportunity to participate in the debate on Bill C-61 which enacts the young offenders act. At this stage of the bill it is appropriate to consider the general principles that underlie it and also some of the specific provisions which ought to be given special consideration.
Before I do that, I wish to make some remarks of a more personal nature. The young offenders act which is to replace the Juvenile Delinquents Act, represents years of evolution with respect to the treatment of young offenders in Canada. In many cases, debate in this House is based upon documented experience, but I have had a long career dealing with juvenile offenders and with the administration of the laws that apply to them. I think it is worth recording that when I commenced my law practice 25 years ago in Halifax, the Juvenile Delinquents Act, which was then the statute in force, did not even apply in the county of Halifax. That particular statute applied at the option of the province in cities and towns and could be excluded in certain places within a province. In 1956 in Halifax county, juveniles did not have the benefit of the Juvenile Delinquents Act but were treated as adult offenders. I give this example to illustrate that while progress is slow, it is made.
One of the reasons there has been such a long period of evolution in the development of law relating to juvenile delinquents is the fact that the Juvenile Delinquents Act was first enacted in 1908 as Chapter 40 of the Statutes of Canada. When one considers the times, it was a relatively thoughtful statutory provision. One of the ideas behind that statutory provision was that it would creat one offence which would apply to all illegal conduct by young persons. That offence was called a "delinquency". The persons who formulated that law at that time had in mind that young persons ought not to be charged in a specific way for the wrongs they might commit or for the violations of laws that might occur.
The idea was to realize that young persons were simply offenders who had breached the law without giving full regard to the exact law that had been breached. It was in this way that the concept of a delinquency was created, and that concept endures to this day. It is a concept that we should not lightly dismiss, that of an offence of delinquency, in favour of a specification of an offence which a young person might commit. That is one thing that we should review very carefully
April 15, 1981

when we consider this bill in the House and in committee. It is a concept that has stood the test of time. There are many who feel that it ought to be changed, but it is still worth careful consideration before that particular change is made.
I was somewhat disturbed by the remarks of the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) when he entered the debate, with the respect to the absence from the House of the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland (Mr. Lawrence). I think it can be said that the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland, as a former solicitor general, has a great interest in this bill. It is unfortunate that he is not able to participate in the debate on second reading because I think he would have a great deal to contribute. I am sure it was with that in mind that the hon. member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn) mentioned the haste with which the bill was brought before the House for consideration, not with the intent of casting any recrimination on anyone, but rather to say that this was an unfortunate occurrence.
I sincerely hope that the Solicitor General has not interfered with the non-partisan spirit that ought to pervade in a debate dealing with young persons in Canada, by interjecting that unfortunate remark. I can say to him that in this very House yesterday when Bill C-58 was called, his colleague, the Presi-dent'of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) was not here to speak to it. He might confer with his colleague and ask him where he was and why he was not present in this House when the bill he sought to have approved on second reading was being considered. When we cast dispersions on other members with respect to their presence or absence from this House, we enter on dangerous ground.
There is one other matter for which I am entitled to take the Solicitor General to task, and that is his suggestion that Bill C-61 ought to pass this House with a minimum of debate and then be considered in committee, presumably the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. I say that because I think all members in this House ought to be very interested in any provision which affects the young people of Canada in such a serious way as this young offenders act does. If any debate was justified in its prolongation in this House so that members could consider and express their thought on such an important measure, surely it is this piece of legislation. Any suggestion that it should be swept through this House with a minimum of debate and discussion is not acceptable to me. In many ways, I think it destroys the credibility of those who seek passage of this bill and approval in this House. The bill is indeed of a non-partisan kind. It was formulated through committees, public discussion and discussion within departments. It was brought forward through previous solicitors general and considered by a great many people. I would certainly like to think that the motivation of those people who dealt with the legislative provisions, now included in Bill C-61, was to improve the situation, create a better law applicable to juveniles and young persons across Canada.
Young Offenders Act
I want to comment briefly on the matter not specifically dealt with by previous speakers and which reflects, to some extent, on the remarks made by the previous speaker. In Canada, we have a very difficult situation, as everyone in this House knows. In their wisdom, the framers of the British North America Act decided to vest in the federal authority, the Parliament of Canada and, the Government of Canada, the right .to enact criminal law legislation. At the same time, the Fathers of Confederation vested in the provinces of Canada the administration of that criminal law. So we have these two elements in the administration of justice in Canada: the federal authority enacting a law, and the provincial authority administering the law.
I say that because a great many remarks relate to the treatment of young persons within provinces whether they are young offenders or whether they are in difficulty of a kind which might involve them with other legal process. Those persons, to a great extent, are the responsibility of the provincial authorities. While we would all seek to have them dealt with in an appropriate and gentle way in order to dissuade them from any unlawful activity in the future, it cannot be a part of this particular bill.
As I understand it, this bill is made by the Parliament of Canada pursuant to its authority to enact criminal law legislation. That is what the bill must deal with. Social justice is a subject which ought to be, and I am sure is, important to all members of this House, but it is a matter which cannot be dealt with effectively as part of the implementation of the authority to enact criminal law.
That leads me, first, to consider briefly the history of Bill C-61, because other members have dealt with it. I want to record thanks for the work of the committee which provided a report in 1975 called the report of the committee on Young Persons in Conflict with the Law. I think it is worth while to refer in specific terms to some of the thoughts which were expressed by the formulators of that report. I should say perhaps that the report was made to the solicitor general of the day, the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. All-mand). The committee was under the direction of the deputy solicitor general of Canada of that time, Mr. Roger Tasse. Contained in the report is a statement which bears recording in this House. Under the heading of "The Challenge of our Times", we read:
Within a modern democratic society, it is neither possible nor desirable to expect that the life styles and behaviour of individuals will conform to a single standard. A society that places a high premium on the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms and prizes material success and rewards individual aspirations, must recognize that the pursuit of such ideals also fosters a diversity in forms of behaviour.
I think that thought was well expressed. Canadians ought to realize they cannot expect from our young persons a standard of conduct or a similarity of behaviour. Our system has to realize and recognize there are those who will not conform to the standard and, for a period of time, hopefully a limited period of time, may find themselves in conflict with the law.
The law we want to formulate in this House is a law which will recognize that difficulty and will deal with it as a social

April 15, 1981
Young Offenders Act
difficulty, not in the frame of mind that we must punish those who, in their youth, find themselves in a difficult situation- although punishment may be a method by which persons are brought to a proper course of action and standard-but to provide a system which redirects the course of those who run afoul of the law.
With that in mind, I want to repeat what I said earlier with respect to the Juvenile Delinquents Act of 1908. It charted a course, which I think has been a very effective one and one which I have watched grow over the years. There are a great many things which can be done to improve the law. We ought to keep that in mind. However, we must recognize that the course which was charted in 1908 is one that we would be wise to follow.
I want to review the provision of Bill C-61 in more detail. First, I want to comment on something which has arisen already in this debate, that is the interrelation of the new young offenders act, enacted by Bill C-61, with the constitutional provisions proposal now before the Parliament of Canada. In very simple terms what I am concerned with is that that constitutional proposal contains a charter of rights. As the heading of the proposal indicates, it guarantees rights and freedoms. One of the freedoms and rights it guarantees is non-discrimination before the law.
I will not detail the provisions of the constitutional proposal other than to say that discrimination is outlawed. I do want to question whether the Government of Canada now seeking to have this proposal approved by this House of Commons and adopted by the Parliament of the United Kingdom and made part of the law of Canada has properly considered those provisions of the charter of rights in relation to laws such as the young offenders act.
I am not questioning the motives of the framers of the provisions of the young offenders act. I am just suggesting to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the members of this House, that this is yet another situation in which the Government of Canada has given evidence that it does not really appreciate, realize or recognize what the effect will be of the charter of rights provisions, or what the effect will be on the people of Canada. In this very bill, as pointed out by previous speakers, the government suggests that there is a provincial option with respect to the application of the act to persons of varying age. Under the provisions of the act, it can be applied to young persons under the age of 18, under the age of 17, or of the age of 16, in accordance with the option selected by a particular province.
Obviously this creates a checkerboard across Canada, as has been mentioned. It creates the possibility of discrimination in relation to the application of a law. It raises the very question with which the charter of rights presumably deals. We question how well thought out this proposal is in relation to the new constitutional provisions.
I want to mention that because there are many other areas I could mention with respect to the application of the charter of rights. Strangely enough, I was present in this House last night when Bill C-58, which amends the Canada Elections Act, was
before the House. That act contains provisions relating to voting rights. At the same time, the constitutional proposal in the charter of rights says that every citizen of Canada has the right to vote in an election. There is another illustration in which the government of Canada has not related the provisions of its constitutional proposal, that is, the specific provisions of the charter of rights, to the provisions which we are considering in this House.
When this comes to the committee, somebody will have to look at this very carefully and decide whether the provisions of Bill C-61 which relate to the age at which the legislative provisions apply to young persons in a province can be enacted in light of those constitutional provisions.
My suggestion in that connection is that what we must have and must look for is flexibility in the law, not a discriminatory provision. The law might be so worded that it can be taken advantage of by certain young persons under 18, that it can be applied at their option, or something of that nature.
I can see where there is a difference of opinion as to whether persons of 17 or 18 years of age ought to be dealt with under the law as young offenders or as adults. However, I do not think that the law should apply differently across Canada. That is something which has caused difficulty in the past. If we are going to remedy the mischiefs of the past, this is the time to do it.
With regard to the provisions of Bill C-61, in relation to the definition of young persons, I suggest that some method be established to provide for flexibility. However, we ought not to start on a course that will result in a different application across Canada. In the case of the government of the day, it is not consistent with the course of action they have adopted with respect to the charter of rights in the constitutional proposal.
I have heard other speakers in this House deal with some of the specifics of the bill. I do not want to repeat what has already been said, but there are a number of matters I would like to deal with very briefly. The first is: the provision under the bill for what is called "alternate measures". This provision simply means that a young offender suspected of violating the law, when brought before the authorities, need not be brought to a youth court, that is to say, a judge of the youth court; he or she can be dealt with in a different way. The bill spells out in what way that person can be dealt with. I want to warn people that this is potentially a very dangerous provision. It is totally dependent on the good faith and good offices of those who administer our criminal law. From my own experience, I think it right and proper for me to suggest that one can have confidence in our law officers across Canada, but there is always the exception that proves the rule. There are those among our law officers whom it may be dangerous to entrust with such power or authority.
Under the previous law, it was possible for a juvenile court judge, when he had a youth before him, to suggest a course of action other than proceeding before that juvenile court. I am not entirely sure that that kind of provision is not more
April 15, 1981

sensible, one that is more likely to avoid any difficulties or mischiefs. I point this out because I know it is of real concern to a number of people who examined the young offenders legislation in its various stages, including the format in which it now appears before this House, namely Bill C-61.
The real pith and substance of this bill is the youth court. The success of the new provisions will rise or fall with the capability of the youth courts across Canada and the persons who act as judges and officers of those youth courts. What we are dealing with in this bill, as in all legislative measures, are people. We can enact any law we want, but if the people do not administer that law fairly and faithfully, the provisions that we enact in this Parliament will go for naught.
I want to examine very briefly the administration of the Juvenile Deliquents Act across Canada in the case of most provinces by the family court or equivalent. In my province of Nova Scotia, as I have indicated, the practice has developed to the point where all juvenile offenders are brought before the family court of Nova Scotia. The family court there, as in many provinces, not only has a legally trained judge, but, in most cases, there are social workers available, as well as psychiatric and other medical help. Indeed, there are other officers who can perform the functions which are required to assess offenders and to chart a course to set them on the road to change. We must recognize very clearly that under this bill the youth court, its function, and the function of its officers will determine the value of this bill when it is enacted and applied across Canada.
Let me point out again that the youth courts are the responsibility of the provinces. When the Solicitor General comes before the House of Commons, presents a bill and sets up a court which is called the youth court, which is merely the family court which has existed and functioned in most provinces for several decades, let us not be fooled that this is an improvement in the law which the Government of Canada is now sponsoring. What the Government of Canada has to provide to create any real effect in an area of this kind is the funds, resources and capabilities which allow for improvements in our provincially constituted and appointed courts such as the family court.
Let us not be fooled into thinking there is any magic in this bill. Let me digress to say that much of my legal career was spent in legislative drafting as legislative counsel for the province of Nova Scotia. I was reminded daily that the laws which we were framing, proposing and enacting would accomplish nothing unless the laws were properly applied. More important, the farther we get away from the basic law, the basic concept of fairness-and, I suggest, the ten commandments are as good a representation of the basic law as you will find-the more difficulties we can create.
I do not want anybody to think that by enacting a new young offenders act with more elaborate provisions and procedures we are resolving the problem. The problem has to be resolved by people, by good faith and by careful consideration of the problems which come before our youth courts and the problems in which the youth courts find themselves involved.
Young Offenders Act
In this connection, mention was made of preventive action. There again we are not referring to the criminal law or criminal justice system but to the whole social justice system. In the many years that I appeared before juvenile and family courts, I have never seen a child who did riot have another problem which was not connected with the criminal justice system. In practically every case, although there were notable exceptions, the child brought before the court had experienced difficulties in his or her family life or educational life causing a departure from standard behaviour. It is only through a competent and effective social justice system that we can remedy these kinds of defects.
Let us not forget the parents. Most offenders who come before family and juvenile courts across this land, with notable exceptions, have difficulty in their family life and in their relationships with their parents. The more serious cases in the provinces can be corrected, or at least dealt with by children protection laws. These laws, as far as I am aware, exist in every province of Canada.
I want to be clear again that we do not discharge our responsibilities by merely enacting and passing in this House of Commons a young offenders act. We have to work to improve our social justice system. We have to work to improve the facilities available through our educational system and through our help to families in need so that the situations which result in proceedings before juvenile and family courts are corrected before they reach that stage.
In that sense, I suppose there is a preventive action involved in our deliberations, but it is very clearly one we cannot successfully deal with in this House of Commons by considering a bill of this kind. As I have said, it is wise for us to keep that in mind.
There has been a long history to the Juvenile Delinquents Act in Canada. I want to call to the attention of members, particularly the Solicitor General, what I believe to be the words of his department, at least to the extent that the publication I will now refer to was preceded by a letter from the Solicitor General.
In that document it is indicated that the word "delinquency" has acquired a pejorative connotation. You will recall that I began my address with an explanation of that word. It is now associated with the word "criminal". In this proposed young offenders act we are moving away from the pejorative term "delinquent".
Let me remind all members of this House that this is exactly what this House of Commons thought it was doing in 1908. Members then thought they were moving away from the treatment then given young offenders. They thought they were moving away and creating a new course of action to be applied to young offenders, and they called that new course of action "delinquency". Some 70 years later we are saying that term has acquired a bad connotation and we are simply moving to other terms, "young offenders" and "youth court". I can tell you, just as sure death and taxes, there will be another House

April 15, 1981
Young Offenders Act
of Commons assembled in 25 years, 50 years or maybe 100 years' time, which will be saying we have to change this young offenders act because it has acquired a terrible connotation. It is now regarded as criminal. It is a terrible thing and nobody wants to be known as a young offender. I know the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) will not be here at that time, and neither will I, but I know it will happen.

I did say in 50 years' time. Let us not fool ourselves and let us not try to fool the public about what we are doing and trying to accomplish here. What we are trying to do is simply to improve the system. We are trying to give the juvenile offender and the system that applies to him a new start. That is all we can do. We can introduce new terms, we can make a few changes, but we have to come to grips with the real and effective provisions of this bill.
To demonstrate why we may not be doing that, let me point out that one of the most offensive provisions of the Juvenile Delinquents Act is that provision under which a juvenile can be transferred to an adult court for prosecution. That is one of the most offensive provisions and this proposed act has hardly changed it. Steven Truscott would still go to trial in an adult court. A 14 or 15-year old who commits murder will still probably be exposed to the regular criminal process. That is how we are coping with some of the problems that arise. That is our great evolution in relation to the Juvenile Delinquents Act. In so many cases we are just changing the label; we are just varying the procedures.
As I said, and I repeat-and let me close on this note-what we have to consider are the people who administer justice as it applies to young persons across Canada. We have to consider the personnel in our youth courts; the judges, the social workers and everybody else. Those are the people who are going to make for a better system of dealing with juvenile offenders. Those are the people who are important, not the law.
We can contribute by giving the administrators of the juvenile justice system, if I can call it that, an instrument through which to apply their abilities, allowing them to help offenders and chart new courses for them. That is all we can do. We can work toward that task. As I have said, this does not involve political parties. It is a non-partisan task because we are working for the people of Canada, and I hope the Solicitor General will keep that in mind.

You will have to be patient for a little while, Mr. Solicitor General. The Solicitor General is calling for the question, Mr. Speaker, but I think he is just a little premature as there are a number on this side of the House who wish to address Bill C-61, the proposed young offenders act.
I should like to preface my main remarks by congratulating the minister. This is his first bill in the House. Although he cannot claim it as his bill because it was formulated by his predecessor, I am sure it is a great experience to introduce and pilot it through the House. I congratulate him and I wish him luck.
I am the first non-lawyer to speak on this subject in the House, and I do not make any apologies for that at all, not one. My responsibility with the Progressive Conservative Party is in respect of the young wing of the party and of youth concerns. I feel it is incumbent upon me to address this House on this legislation, a bill which has some very long term ramifications for our justice system.
Let me start by saying we agree with the concept of greater rights, greater responsibilities and greater flexibility in dealing with the rehabilitation of young offenders. This is a very good concept. It is long overdue. I am not even going to touch on the subject of its history as that has been covered by my colleagues.
I should like to touch upon a few subjects, the first being age. Under Clause 2(1) of Bill C-61, a child is defined as being anyone who is or appears to be under the age of 12 years; it defines a young person as anyone who is or appears to be over the age of 12 and under the age of 18.
There is also a provision in the same clause that the governor-in-council may issue a proclamation at the request of a province to establish the maximum age of a young person as being either under the age of 17 or 16 years.
The consequence of this provision is that the youth court would have exclusive jurisdiction in respect of an offence committed by a young person between the ages of 12 and 16, or 17 or 18. A person under the age of 12 is to be subject to provincial child welfare legislation. Where the individual is over the age of 16, 17 or 18, he would be subject to ordinary criminal law and the jurisdiction of the ordinary courts.
The change effected by Bill C-61 is that the minimum age of jurisdiction of the youth court is to be increased from 7 to 12 years, and the maximum age is to be increased from 16 to 18 years with the possibility of a reduction rather than an increase, as is presently the case under the Juvenile Delinquents Act.
The effect of increasing the minimum age is that the youth population which will be subject to provincial laws and social welfare programs alone will increase dramatically. This will put a tremendous additional cost on the provinces. Of course, we are interested to find out if there is any increased funding in view of the shuffling off of these responsibilities to the social welfare programs of the provinces. It also would have the effect of decriminalizing any delinquent acts committed by those who are under the minimum age. The effect of raising the maximum age would be to increase the number of young people who would be subject to the juvenile justice system at the upper age limit and require that a province request explicitly that this be reduced. Despite many attempts over the years to establish a uniform maximum age across the country, the
April 15, 1981

federal and provincial governments have been unable to come to an agreement on this issue, and I think that is unfortunate.
The inequity in our justice system across the country has been well covered today. People will be treated differently because of their ages. In fact, we know that the current age level in the various provinces and territories is as follows: in Quebec and Manitoba the age is 18 years; in British Columbia the age is 17 years; in all the remaining provinces and territories the age is 16 years. In Newfoundland, where the Juvenile Delinquents Act does not apply, the age under provincial legislation is 17 years.

Sixteen and a half, is it? The Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) is at least following my remarks, and I am pleased about that.
Despite these many attempts, we have been unable to do it, and I hope we can address that particular problem in committee. I tend to agree with my colleagues when they say that this will have serious ramifications on equality of law in the country.
One of the concerns which has been expressed to me by those people who deal with the courts is that there is no provision and no option for those under the age of 12 who do get into trouble with the law and whose cases perhaps should be referred to a youth court. There is no provision for that. We heard today about examples of young people to whom an appearance in family court in all likelihood would be to their advantage and for their well-being, but that will not happen, and I think the minister should examine some of the cases in the province of Quebec. In fact, he mentioned this in his address. In some of these cases in Quebec social workers have handled young people under 12 exclusively and have not referred them to the court. Some of the stories are somewhat disturbing. I hope that is something we will look at in the committee and discuss fully. We should discuss whether an option should be provided to a child under the age of 12 who is a chronic problem. Perhaps such cases can be referred to family courts if it is felt that that is necessary. I cannot see how that would be possible under this bill, unless provincial governments set up other courts to handle these problems or institute legislation giving them the power to refer cases to family courts.
The present Juvenile Delinquents Act does not define offences covered in the legislation as such, but defines as a juvenile delinquent a person between the ages of 7 and 16. The youth court would have jurisdiction now under Bill C-61- which has, as I said, reduced dramatically the number of offences for which a young person could be brought before the youth court-with respect to federal offences only. Under Bill C-61, any violations of provincial or municipal law or any status offences would be subject to provincial child welfare and child protection legislation.
Young Offenders Act
The differences in philosophies between the present Juvenile Delinquents Act and Bill C-61 are most apparent in the social welfare approach of the Juvenile Delinquents Act and the alternate measures we find in Bill C-61. The declaration of principles in the Juvenile Delinquents Act, as I said, takes a social welfare approach by which concerns about the behaviour of young people is expressed, and the courts merely provide a means by which social intervention can take place to deal with the family and environmental causes which lead to alleged delinquent behaviour.
The declaration of principles in Bill C-61 constitutes a somewhat different approach for dealing with young people. First, the new legislation would cover specific acts committed by young people and not their behaviour as such. Second, the declaration of principles recognizes some of the contradictions inherent in applying criminal law sanctions to situations in which individual acts take place in particular socio-economic environments. It recognizes that there are not only individual rights to be protected but also that the social impact of certain acts must be minimized. It recognizes the due process rights of young people but also their responsibilities, as well as those of the family and society.
There is a number of concerns with respect to this legislation about which I want to talk for just a moment. I know they will be discussed more fully in the committee. In this legislation there is no provision for contributing to juvenile delinquency. This has caused some concern, mainly because the acts of a person who contributes to juvenile delinquency will be dealt with in a senior court, and young people will probably in many instances be the only witnesses and will have to testify in senior courts. Clause 60 of Bill C-61, a new clause, covers evidence of a child or a young person and solemn affirmations. This is an excellent clause. I recommend to the minister that it be incorporated into the Criminal Code. If an individual is charged with contributing to juvenile delinquency, perhaps young witnesses will have to appear as the only witnesses in senior courts.
My colleague, the hon. member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn), touched on differences in ages. Many solutions have been offered. One suggested solution was the option of petitioning a family court to be heard in a higher court for a particular offence. In those areas where juveniles are those people under the age of 16, it could conceivably be that people 17 and 18 might have the option of petitioning higher courts to be heard in family courts. That is another option at which the minister and his officials will look.
The old act allows a family court judge to direct that a child be put into the custody of a municipality or a children's aid society and to direct that certain payments be made to cover the care and protection of that young person. That provision has disappeared now as well. I realize that that will now be under provincial jurisdiction. I expect that it will be under the jurisdiction of a director, who would be under the jurisdiction of the attorney general or the solicitor general of a province. It would be his duty to take care of that particular individual, but that is an option which we have now taken away. We are

April 15, 1981
Young Offenders Act
narrowing the scope judges have and this, of course, could be extremely dangerous.
There are many other points I want to cover, but I will not do that today. I might, however, deal with perhaps four or five briefly. I know another colleague wants to speak before we call it six o'clock. I will cover a number of situations when we get to the committee.
There are a number of provisions in the present Juvenile Delinquents Act which do not have their equivalent in Bill C-61 and hence are repealed. There is no equivalent in Bill C-61 to Section 17 of the present act which indicates that proceedings are to be informal and are not be affected by any irregularity based upon that informality. Section 22 of the Juvenile Delinquents Act provides that where a parent or guardian has conduced to the commission of an offence by a young person by neglecting to exercise due care of that person, he may be ordered to pay a fine, damages or costs. This section is repealed and is not replaced by an equivalent in the new legislation. In other words, parents will no longer be held responsible for the acts of young people.
Section 23 of the Juvenile Delinquents Act provides that a child's religion is to be respected when he is placed in any foster home or any other residence. There is no equivalent in Bill C-61. I hope it is covered somewhere else, and I hope a child's religion is respected when he is placed in the care of a foster home or whatever. I do not see that provision in this bill. I hope the minister will deal with it in committee.
Sections 27 to 28 of the Juvenile Delinquents Act deal with the creation of a juvenile court committee. These sections are repealed and are not replaced. Section 33 of the act makes it an offence for anyone to have contributed to juvenile delinquency. Sections 34 provides a penalty for inducing a child to leave an institution to which he has been sent by the juvenile court. There are no equivalents to these sections in Bill C-61. I am sure the minister will give these answers in committee.
In summation, we have concerns with this act. We will go to committee with some suggestions. Hopefully the minister will call expert witnesses and will accept suggestions from our side of the House as to who some of those witnesses will be. Hopefully we will carry this bill through, not hastily but wisely, and will bring forward a piece of legislation which will benefit young people of Canada, will provide proper protection of the victims, as well as proper sentencing and care of young offenders so that they will be returned to society, rehabilitated into worth-while and contributing Canadian citizens.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to make a contribution to this debate. I am particularly indebted to the hon. member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid). I know there were other matters in the legislation with which he was concerned, but in order to provide me with a few minutes, he very kindly gave up some of his time.
I understand the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) wanting to get this piece of legislation through quickly at this stage, most ministers feel that way. In fact, I am not sure it is necessarily in anyone's interest to be overly hasty. I do not foresee second reading debate going on day after day, week after week. But I think it is the type of legislation which would not necessarily attract the public attention I would like to see it attract. Sometimes when very bad legislation is drafted, by its very nature it will attract public outcry. Indeed, that happened around 1970 when we were considering this type of legislation.
One advantage of second reading going on for a reasonable length of time is that it brings to the attention of various individuals, groups, organizations and agencies, a matter with which they may not have been otherwise preoccupied, a matter in which they should demonstrate some interest.
We have lived with the present act for over 70 years. There have been no substantial changes since 1929, over 50 years ago. I received the information package from the minister last February. I circulated it in my riding among judges, people working with young offenders and lawyers practising that type of law. I have not received much response to it. Perhaps it is because it is good legislation. I think it generally is. The Solicitor General understands that most of us on this side feel that way, but I hope that as the process develops, if there are concerns out there, that we will receive responses.
I think it is very important for people, such as the hon. member for Brampton-Georgetown who is not a lawyer, to participate. Those of us who are lawyers see this as a movement in the judicial process, from the old act to the new one, and are quite comfortable with it as a process. People who are not lawyers often look at the substance of the change in a much different light. Therefore, I encourage participation on all sides of the House by those who do not necessarily belong to the legal profession.
It is amazing that the present act has stood up as well as it has, considering the social, economic and cultural changes which have occurred since 1929, especially in the past three decades. I think "amazing" is the proper word. It is likely attributable to juvenile court judges and provincial authorities and agencies responsible. During this period of time, I suppose they have taken some poetic licence with the act which had not changed as society changed.
The juvenile court was put in a very unusual position because it was not only adjudicating, it was part of the treatment process. Court officials are not necessarily trained or inclined to be part of the treatment process. Therefore, when the minister paid particular tribute to the juvenile court judges and provincial authorities in his information booklet, I very much agreed and seconded those kind of remarks. If this legislation is any indicia, with good intention and every justification, we have likely infringed upon what is commonly known as basic rights and freedoms. Perhaps it was inevitable and not a matter of public controversy because the courts are closed. I suppose, as part of the treatment process, certain licence had to be taken. It was difficult for the court to be part of the treatment process. Given the legal confines regarding rights
April 15, 1981

and freedoms, the two roles, challenges and responsibilities could not be discharged satisfactorily.
The legislation changes the role of the court significantly from a treatment agency to one of a legal function. It is not simply a legal function in adjudicating guilt or innocence. As an aside, I have always found the adjudicating function in the present system to be rather difficult because the adjudication consisted of asking: Is this young person a juvenile delinquent? There were many guidelines for this, but it was almost as difficult as an adult court asking: "Is this accused an habitual criminal?" The meaning of the words was broad.
Another legal function which will be given to the court under this new legislation is to define the responsibility of the intervention flowing from the disposition. When I say "intervention", I mean the agency or the person who picks up once the disposition has been made, whether it is custody, probation, restitution or community service. There is no awarding of wardship, as I understand it, compared to the present act. Therefore, we do not have a situation where intervening agencies could extend or increase the period of control. It is desirable, indeed essential, that the court establish the maximum degree and length of the intervention. It is also desirable, although it may not be essential, that the agent can initiate the lessening of that period but should not increase it without a reference back to the court. This is recognized in the bill before us.
Before dealing with some other parts of the legislation, I want to emphasize one concern which bothers me more than any other, that is, the relationship between the two levels of government in this area. First, the minister in referring to committee talked about expert witnesses appearing before that committee. I concur in that. But he did not say that this would include the provincial perspective. I believe it is incumbent upon the Solicitor General to not only permit provincial witnesses, but, I think, he has a responsibility to enlist provincial witnesses at the committee stage. This may not be a good analogy, but I went through a similar type of procedure in committee with respect to the Fisheries Act. That act is federal legislation and administered in certain provinces by provincial authorities. We were assured in committee that extensive consultations had taken place. Indeed, they had. But unfortunately the federal government consulted with one and not both of the two provincial elements which were concerned-environment and fisheries. Therefore, while there had been consultation and concurrence on the one arm of the provincial government, the second group was never consulted. The second group was very upset with this legislation. They came before committee at the last minute and made a very strong plea for substantial changes to the legislation. I do not want to see a repeat of this. It was unnecessary. It caused unnecessary delay to important legislation. We did not have the proper amendments because it became very much an adversary approach between the two levels of government. Therefore, at the committee stage I hope we will hear from provincial governments. We do not need to hear from ten. I
