presume there is a community of interest and a consensus there so that we can hear from one spokesman what the problems or criticisms are.
I agree with what everyone has said about a serious attempt being made to set a common maximum age. I do not think I need dwell on that subject any longer. But there is a serious shortcoming. Given this government's track record with respect to federal-provincial relations, I very much doubt that a serious attempt to set a uniform age has been undertaken.
I think we must plug some gaps in the system which are created by the legislation since it only deals with offences under the Criminal Code, offences under federal legislation and regulations. It does not deal with provincial legislation. It does not deal with municipal ordinances and bylaws. Looking at the latest statistics available from Statistics Canada from the justice statistics division, I noted that there were somewhere in excess of 6,000 cases in 1979 which dealt with legislation other than federal legislation, in other words, provincial and municipal. These 6,000 cases were cases where the young person was found to be a juvenile delinquent. I am not sure if the machinery exists in the provinces to immediately fill the gap which would be created upon Royal Assent being granted to this legislation. Therefore, I think the provinces need some time. I would like to know from the Solicitor General at the committee stage how much time will be needed to fill that particular gap. I am concerned because I am told that in certain provinces the system is already overcrowded in many of its parts.
I am also concerned with the provision for children under the age of 12. Again, looking at the figures of the justice statistics division, I find that over 2,300 persons were found delinquent who were 11 years of age or under. Of the 2,300, over 2,000 were offences under the Criminal Code. Therefore, by raising the age from seven to 12 I believe another gap will be created.
I point out to the Solicitor General that I find the same trouble as he, I am sure, with respect to statistics dealing with juvenile delinquency. They are not terribly reliable and the reporting system is bad. I sympathize with him but I cannot offer him any assistance. I am very concerned about the gaps that are created mainly for provincial governments as a result of this legislation. I am delighted that my colleague from Halifax raised this because I find the same trouble as he with this diversion or alternate measures system contained in section 4 of the act. I find it very vague. For example, in the information brochure which my colleague was looking at, the question posed is: Will every young person who breaks a federal law appear in the youth court? The answer given is "Not necessarily". The minister goes on to deal with this alternative measures provision. It says that these programs which are called diversion programs may entail community service involvement, special education programs, counselling and restitution agreements. The common characteristic is that they are all voluntary. There is nothing about that in the legislation.

I agree with my colleague that, the key instrument here is the person who is considering whether to use such measures, that is, the alternative measures. This could be a very bad flaw. I do not know if there is a way to make this less vague, but I find it terribly vague. In the hands of an unscrupulous person, agency or authority, some very serious consequences could flow from this section.
I understand that there is an escape provision. I agree with that. Certainly if the accused does not wish to go that route, he cannot be forced to. I again emphasize that the abuse of the measure under subsection (5) is no bar to future proceedings. My main quarrel with that provision is its vagueness on the one hand and, on the other hand, I do not see the checks and balances which I would like to see in terms of the exercise of authority by the person who initiates the alternative measure process.
I am again assisted by my colleague from Halifax who has had much more experience with this subject than I have. There is no indication in Section 4 that the young person has been advised by legal counsel in terms of agreeing to take the alternative measures route. I think the Solicitor General will have to deal with that at the committee stage and assure us that this is the best he can do. I know diversion is a key element of the whole program, and I support that. But I have some very serious questions about that particular section and its efficacy procedures.
There was one other matter I wanted to raise with the Solicitor General. I believe I have only a minute left in which
to do it. This is a question on which maybe the Solicitor General will drop me a note or about which he will speak to me privately. The principles here are very important because it says that the act shall be interpreted in light of them. I do not understand the difference between responsibility and accountability. It says that one of the principles is that the offender shall be responsible but not necessarily accountable. I am a lawyer and I have played with words for a good number of years and I cannot get around that particular aspect of the act. But it is a small point.
This is the final point I wish to make. I understand the need to eliminate truancy, incorrigibility and sexual immorality. I know the capricious nature that has often resulted in a person appearing before the court, but there are some very desperate parents out there who have legitimately used this provision from time to time. I do not know where parents can turn at this point.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

It being six o'clock p.m., the House stands adjourned until Tuesday, April 21, 1981 at two o'clock p.m.
May I add that the Speaker extends the usual invitation to hon. members and the staff to enjoy some hospitality in Room 16. I hope it is possible for all hon. members and members of the staff to attend.
At six o'clock the House adjourned, without question put, pursuant to Standing Order.
